latest.headline: Revenue up 26%, operating profit flat, and the margin guidance came down.
body: Suzlon reported its July-September quarter on 29 October 2026. Revenue rose 26% to ₹4,869 crore on a record 710 MW of turbine deliveries (a megawatt is how turbine capacity is counted). Reported profit fell 69% to ₹394 crore. The stock fell about 10% the next day, to a 52-week low near ₹33.

Do not read that 69% literally. A year ago, profit included an ₹891 crore tax credit: the company booked, in one go, the value of old losses it can use to cut future tax bills. That does not repeat. Take it out and profit was roughly flat, ₹394 crore against about ₹389 crore.

The real problem is the margin. Suzlon brought in about ₹1,000 crore more revenue than a year ago and kept none of it as extra operating profit. EBITDA (profit from running the business, before interest, tax and depreciation) was ₹720 crore, the same as last year, so the margin fell from 18.6% to 14.8%. On the turbines alone, the contribution margin (what is left from each machine after its direct costs) fell from 26.9% to 21.2%. Coverage blamed a heavier mix of full turnkey projects, where Suzlon also builds the site at thinner margins, plus commodity and currency swings. Management cut its FY27 EBITDA margin guidance to 15-16%, from about 17%.

Two things to watch next. UBS flagged that operating cash flow for April-September was negative, about ₹200 crore, even with ₹2,048 crore of net cash on the balance sheet and a fresh CRISIL upgrade to AA-. And the October-December quarter will show whether the margin settles inside the new guidance or keeps sliding.

oneLiner: Suzlon came back from near-bankruptcy to become India's biggest wind maker, and it is now net cash. Survival is settled. What is not settled is whether margins that have slipped two quarters running come back as the business grows.

verdict.keyQuestion: Survival is settled. Margins have slipped two quarters running. Is that the cost of moving into bigger turnkey projects, or the new normal?

facts.snapshot: Suzlon Energy is India's largest wind-turbine maker. It builds and sells wind turbines, then earns recurring fees servicing them over their roughly twenty-year life on the hillsides where they spin.

overview: Suzlon makes the giant wind turbines you see spinning on India's ridgelines, and every machine it sells has two lives. The first is loud: it builds and sells the turbine, a lumpy order-book business that booms and busts with government auctions and corporate capex. The second is quiet: once the blades are up on a hillside, the owner keeps paying Suzlon to service them and keep them spinning for twenty years or more. That second life is the gem. Suzlon is the largest wind maker in India, with roughly 29% of everything ever installed and a fleet of about 15.7 GW under its care. After a decade on the brink, it is net cash. Survival is settled. What is not settled is what you pay for the recovery, and whether a project-heavy business can grow fast without its margins and its cash conversion slipping.

editorial.realBusiness: Suzlon is not a turbine you buy once. It is a machine sold once and then serviced for twenty years, on a fleet it rarely loses.
editorial.whyExists: India has promised a vast renewable build-out, and wind is the harder half of it: heavy engineering, giant logistics, a service tail measured in decades. Suzlon deserves to exist because it is the only Indian player with the scale, the in-house factories and the nationwide service crews to put turbines up and then keep them running for twenty years.
editorial.whyNotAlreadyWon: Because wind is brutally cyclical and the technology keeps moving. Suzlon was nearly killed once, by debt piled on at the top of a cycle and by falling behind on turbine size. Leadership here has to be won again every product generation, and a weak balance sheet simply does not survive the down-leg.

mentalModels.why: Heavy fixed manufacturing base: volume drops through hard once plants are full, and hurts hard when they are not.
The installed fleet pays Suzlon to maintain it for 20+ years, a sticky, higher-quality income stream.
Turbine demand swings with auctions, policy and capex cycles, not a smooth line.
In-house blades, nacelles, towers and forgings protect cost and supply, but also lock in fixed cost.
Going from ₹12,000 cr of debt to net cash is the single biggest change in the story.
Falling behind on turbine size once nearly ended the company; the risk never fully goes away.

winningToday: A ~6 GW order book gives multi-year revenue visibility, most of it from PSU and corporate buyers.
The balance sheet went from near-fatal debt to net cash, which changes the risk of the whole business.
Revenue more than doubled in two years as deliveries ramped, so the recovery is real, not just guided.
The 20-year service book on a 15.7 GW fleet earns ~40% margins and is harder for rivals to displace once Suzlon's turbines are up.
stopWinning: A wind capex slowdown, or slower auctions, would hit turbine volumes and expose the fixed-cost base.
Scaling fast is squeezing margins and cash: in H1 FY27 revenue grew about 24% while EBITDA did not grow at all.
Falling behind on turbine technology, as it did before, would be the deepest wound.
Working capital is building; debtor days rose to 137, and a project business can trap cash quickly.
marketBets: India's wind installations keep accelerating and auctions stay healthy.
Suzlon holds product and cost leadership against better-funded rivals.
The ramp-up margin dip is temporary, not the start of competitive-bid pressure.
Cash conversion catches up with reported profit as execution matures.

sectorModels.note: Strong in corporate and service deals, weak in competitive-bid auctions.
Turbine demand is lumpy and policy-driven, not a smooth compounding line.
The installed-fleet O&M book is durable and sticky for two decades.
From ₹12,000 cr debt to net cash; the biggest single improvement in the story.
Turbine size and design cycles can strand a laggard, as history proved here.

editorial.whyNow: The stock is down about 35% over the past year and sits near a three-year low. The reason is not the order book, which is still about 6 GW. It is that the margin dip everyone hoped was a one-quarter blip in Q1 FY27 showed up again in Q2, and management then cut its own margin guidance for the year. A market that paid up for a clean recovery is now asking whether turnkey projects and tougher bids have reset what Suzlon earns on each turbine. If the margin settles at 15-16% and cash turns positive, the lower price starts to look interesting. If it keeps sliding, nearly 5x book still has room to fall. The lenses below break it down.
editorial.remember: Suzlon is a genuine redemption story now priced like a growth stock. Judge it on cash conversion and whether the margins hold at scale, not on the order-book headline.

ipoFlag: No repackaging games. Suzlon has been listed since 2005 and is the same wind company it always was. Its history is the warning, not its name: read the case study on how debt and a technology miss nearly ended it.

moneyFlow.intro: The business is two flows stacked on one machine. Follow them down.

steps.label: Sell the turbine
steps.value: A PSU or corporate buyer pays for megawatts of wind capacity, booked as a lumpy project

steps.label: Install the fleet
steps.value: Suzlon's blades, towers and nacelles go up, adding to a 15.7 GW base it built

steps.label: Service it for 20 years
steps.value: The owner keeps paying Suzlon a recurring fee to maintain and run those turbines

moneyFlow.spread: The turbine sale is the loud, cyclical revenue everyone watches. The quiet service fee on the whole installed fleet is the annuity that makes Suzlon more than a boom-bust manufacturer. Value both, but weight the durable one.

business.unitOfRevenue: A megawatt of wind turbine sold up front, then a recurring service fee on that same turbine for twenty years or more. The machine sale is lumpy and driven by the order book. The service tail is smooth and sticky. Suzlon also earns from its own forging and foundry operations that feed the turbines.
business.revenueModel: Project-based turbine sales, booked as deliveries against a multi-year order book, plus long-term operations-and-maintenance contracts on the installed fleet. The recurring service revenue rides on top of every machine Suzlon has ever sold.

segments.name: Turbine projects (RE Projects)
segments.marginProfile: of revenue · ~13% EBITDA margin (Fathom approx). The volume engine: lumpy, cyclical, thinner on competitive-bid orders.

segments.name: Service annuity (O&M)
segments.marginProfile: of revenue · 40.5% EBITDA margin (company-reported, FY26). Recurring on a 15.7 GW fleet, with contractual price escalation.

business.revenuePerUnitTrend: Here is the one thing to understand about Suzlon, and most beginners miss it: a rupee of turbine revenue and a rupee of service revenue are not worth the same. In FY26 the O&M service book earned a ~40.5% EBITDA margin. The turbine business earns only low-teens. So ₹100 of service revenue drops roughly three times as much profit as ₹100 of turbine revenue. That is why the mix matters more than the headline growth rate. The service fee is also the steadier line, contractual with built-in price escalation, and it grows on its own as the fleet grows. Turbine prices swing with the order mix: corporate and PSU deals hold, competitive-bid auctions do not. What you watch is whether the blended margin holds as fast-growing turbine volume outpaces the steadier service book, because the first half of FY27 showed it can slip hard. Segment splits are approximate reads of the mix, not exact disclosures.

industry.structure: Consolidating oligopoly in Indian wind. A handful of serious original-equipment makers, with Suzlon the domestic leader by installed base.
industry.competitors: TPG-backed (formerly Siemens Gamesa India), Envision, GE and Wind World are the main rivals. Suzlon leads on cumulative installed share (~29%) and India service depth; some rivals have deeper pockets and global technology.
industry.pricingPower: Split. Real in corporate and service contracts, weak in government competitive-bid auctions where price is the deciding factor.
industry.demandDriver: India's renewable capacity build-out toward a 500 GW non-fossil target, with wind re-accelerating after years of solar dominance. Structural in direction, but delivered through lumpy, policy-driven auctions.
industry.driverType: Structural demand growth delivered through a cyclical, auction-driven order flow.
industry.tam: A large and growing Indian wind market as the country races to add renewable capacity, but one where annual installs swing with policy and financing cycles rather than compounding smoothly.
industry.penetration: Wind is under-built relative to targets, so there is a long runway, but the runway is walked in uneven steps set by auction calendars.
industry.valueChainPosition: The manufacturer and lifetime service provider, the seat that keeps both the build margin and the annuity, spending heavily on plants and working capital to hold it.

business.qualityVerdict: As a turnaround, Suzlon is genuinely impressive: net cash after near-death, the clear domestic leader, a real service annuity throwing off ~40% margins, and a strong recovery in the cycle. But be honest about the industry it lives in. Wind manufacturing is cyclical, capital-hungry, and part price-capped by auctions, and the eye-catching 40% ROE is flattered by a thin post-restructuring equity base. So this is a strong operator in a hard, lumpy business. The service book is the durable, high-margin core. The turbine business is the volume that sets the swings.

cashFlowNote: This is the honest soft spot in an otherwise strong story. Reported FY26 profit was ₹3,163 cr, but operating cash flow was only ₹1,202 cr, so barely 38 paise of every rupee of profit actually showed up as cash. Part of that gap is tax credits that lifted profit without bringing in any cash. Free cash flow is still positive at ₹626 cr after capex, and the balance sheet is genuinely net cash, so this is not a solvency worry. But the gap, together with debtor days climbing to 137, is the classic sign of a fast-scaling project business tying up cash in working capital. The number to watch is whether cash conversion catches up with profit as the order book converts.

growth.label: Profit CAGR 3Y
growth.hint: meaningless: FY22 loss + FY23 one-off base

management: Chairman and MD Vinod Tanti anchors a promoter family that once brought the company to the edge, and a professional bench now runs the business, with Ajay Kapur brought in as CEO to drive the next leg. Credit where it is due: this team pulled off one of the hardest balance-sheet repairs the Indian market has seen, converting debt to equity, raising ₹2,000 cr, and taking the company from ₹12,000 cr of borrowings to net cash. That is a real scorecard. Two things temper it. Promoter ownership is now low at 11.70%, after years of dilution and restructuring, so the family has modest skin in the game and governance leans on the professional board. And the job now changes: from fixing the balance sheet to running a much bigger business profitably, and the first half of FY27 already showed margins and cash can lag when the volume runs hard.

sources: Largest Indian wind installed base (~29% cumulative share)
20-year O&M service annuity on a 15.7 GW fleet
Vertical integration: in-house blades, nacelles, towers, forgings
Nationwide service force of 4,000+ hard to replicate
moat.note: The moat is not the turbine, which rivals can build too. It is the installed fleet and the service crews wrapped around it: once Suzlon's machines are up, the owner tends to keep paying Suzlon to run them, and that book only grows as the fleet grows. The numbers back it up. The O&M business earns a reported 40.5% EBITDA margin on a 15.7 GW base, with contractual price escalation built in. The honest caveat is what the moat does not defend. It does not stop a better-funded rival winning the next auction on price. Service contracts can in principle be re-tendered. And it does nothing against a technology cycle, which is exactly the flank that wounded Suzlon before. Narrow, genuinely strong in service, and exposed on the manufacturing side.

narrative: For a decade Suzlon was the cautionary tale of Indian markets: a 2007-08 global buying spree funded with dollar debt, a technology cycle it fell behind on, and a balance sheet that buckled under roughly ₹12,000 cr of borrowings. Then the story flipped. A debt-for-equity restructuring and a ₹2,000 cr raise cleaned up the balance sheet, India's renewable push pulled wind demand back, and deliveries ramped hard. Revenue went from ₹6,529 cr in FY24 to ₹16,732 cr in FY26, profit turned durable, and the company reached net cash. The stock rose 5x into 2025 on that recovery, then lost more than a third of its value over the following year as the market started questioning margins and valuation. One caution on the numbers: FY23's eye-catching 48% profit margin was a restructuring one-off, and even the ~19% of FY25 and FY26 was helped by tax credits. The cleaner read is the operating margin (profit from running the business, before interest and tax), which was 17-18% in those two years.
risks: Cyclicality and auction dependence. Turbine demand is lumpy and set by government auction calendars and capex cycles, so a slow year hits volumes and exposes the fixed-cost base. High.

Margin and cash at scale. EBITDA margin fell to 14.8% in Q2 FY27 and FY27 guidance was cut to 15-16%; FY26 operating cash was only 38% of profit, and H1 FY27 operating cash flow was negative. Medium-High.
Technology cycle. Turbine size and design keep advancing; falling behind, as Suzlon did before, is the deepest structural risk in this business. Medium.
Low promoter holding. At 11.70%, the family has limited skin in the game and a history of distress-driven selling, so governance leans on the professional board. Medium.
Valuation. Nearly 5x book and ~22x earnings for a cyclical manufacturer leaves little room if the recovery in margins or cash conversion disappoints. Medium-High.

summary: Suzlon is a rare and genuine turnaround: the near-dead debt casualty of the last cycle is now India's net-cash wind leader, with a ~6 GW order book and a sticky 20-year service annuity. None of that is in doubt. What is in doubt is the margin, now two quarters into a slide. You are paying nearly 5 times book and about 22 times earnings for a business that is cyclical, part price-capped by auctions, and whose own management just lowered what it expects to earn on each rupee of sales this year. If the margin settles at the new guidance and cash catches up, the de-rated price is interesting. If it keeps sliding, the multiple has room to fall. The next few quarters will tell you which it is: the cost of moving into bigger projects, or weaker economics at the new size. Not a buy or sell call. Do your own work and consult a SEBI-registered adviser.

engine.earnings: The engine ran hard on the delivery ramp: FY26 revenue up ~54%, on record turbine volumes and a growing service book. FY27 so far is a different picture. Revenue is still growing, up about 24% in the first half, but operating profit has stopped growing with it (see the note at the top for the quarter). The trailing profit line looks worse than it is: reported profit is down 29% over the last twelve months, but that is mostly last year's tax credits dropping out, and profit before tax is up about 18%. The tailwind is real, a ~6 GW order book converting toward management's 25% growth guidance. So is the drag from thinner turnkey margins and working capital.
engine.multiple: Here is a quirk worth understanding. Since August the price fell from about ₹48 to ₹36, yet the P/E went up, from ~21x to ~22x. How? The old P/E was measured against earnings padded by one-time tax credits. Those have now dropped out of the trailing twelve months, so earnings per share fell from ₹2.33 to ₹1.66, faster than the price. The good news is that today's ~22x is on fully taxed profit, so it is a cleaner number. The bad news is that it is not cheap for a cyclical manufacturer whose margins are going the wrong way. Price to book fell to ~4.8x, and that move is real.
engine.verdict: My honest read: the turnaround itself is done and real, but the price was built on the recovery scaling cleanly, and the first half of FY27 broke that assumption. One bad quarter could be a ramp dip. Two, plus a guidance cut, means management itself expects thinner margins this year. What I cannot tell you is whether that is a temporary cost of moving into turnkey projects or the start of tougher pricing at scale, and neither can anyone yet. So watch two numbers over the next couple of quarters: the blended margin against the new 15-16% guidance, and whether operating cash flow turns positive.

lenses.name: The tremor came back
lenses.reading: Q1 FY27 was the first quarter in this recovery where more revenue did not bring more profit, and it was easy to call it a blip. Q2 repeated it, with the margin a notch lower again (the numbers are in the note at the top). Part of the reason is a choice: Suzlon is taking on more full turnkey projects, 38% of the order book now with a 50% target by FY28, and building the whole site earns a thinner margin than selling the machine. Part is not a choice: commodity and currency swings. Is a lower margin on bigger projects a bad trade? Not necessarily, if profit in rupees still grows. In H1 FY27 it did not. Until it does, treat the tremor as a trend.

lenses.name: The turn, remembered
lenses.reading: This is the same company our case study calls 'the sadness': debt and a technology miss nearly ended it, and clearing the debt by printing new shares saved the company but left the 2008 shareholder behind. The redemption is real. So is the memory. The durable edge is the service fleet, not the turbine, and the old wound, being outbuilt on technology, is still the flank to guard.

lenses.name: The growth is not reaching cash yet
lenses.reading: FY26 turned ₹3,163 cr of reported profit into only ₹1,202 cr of operating cash, and debtor days keep climbing toward 137. The business is genuinely net cash, so this is a working-capital drag, not a fraud flag. But it is the number that tells you whether the growth is compounding into cash or just booking revenue. The first half of FY27 went the wrong way: operating cash flow was negative, about ₹200 cr, according to UBS. Until operating cash catches up with profit, treat the reported earnings as running ahead of the money the business actually throws off.

lenses.name: Operator meeting the scale test
lenses.reading: Management earned trust by pulling off a brutal balance-sheet repair, an operator's achievement, not a storyteller's. The next test is a different one: running a much larger, faster-growing manufacturer profitably. Judge them on margin and cash at scale, not on the order-book headline.
